newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Export boost key to Czech crown stability - report.
newsitem.headline: Export boost key to Czech crown stability - report.

text.p: The Czech government needs to take steps to boost exports if currency stability is to be sustained over time, investment firm Merrill Lynch said.
It said an offensive was needed on three fronts -- wages, and fiscal and supply side policy -- in order to stimulate exports and retain the crown's strength
"Exports need to be stimulated if the foundations for stable and sustained growth are to be established, and if the currency is to be preserved at current levels over the longer term."
The Czech Republic is running a large trade deficit and its current account deficit could reach 5.7 percent of gross domestic product in 1996.

On Thursday, Czech business daily Hospodarske Noviny quoted Industry Minister Vladimir Dlouhy as saying the current account deficit could reach crisis proportions next year if current trends continue.
But the report said the central bank's foreign currency reserves -- nearly $13 billion in July -- should be sufficient to steady the market in the event the crown lost current support..
"Even if the currently bullish support for the Koruna (crown) evaporates, the Czech Republic should still have sufficient foreign exchange reserves to steady the market."
However, the investment bank said the government needed to take firm action to improve economic fundamentals, which would in turn help exports, if a devaluation is to be avoided in the longer term.
While praiseworthy of the crown, the report was less than glowing about Prime Minster Vaclav Klaus's free market rhetoric, saying the country lagged other reforming states in economic restructuring.
"For all the Thatcherite rhetoric, the Klaus government has not exposed the economy to unfettered market forces," the report said.
"Compared to other Central European nations, the Czech Republic has proved dilatory in restructuring enterprises in order to improve efficiency," it added.
